selected.name: Long scaffolding erected for one terminal pun
selected.instruction: Score the ratio of setup material to payoff. 10 = several sentences or paragraphs of narrative, list, or verse exist for no reason other than to make one final pun grammatical, and each setup clause is transparently reverse-engineered from the punchline. 5 = moderate setup, some of which does independent work. 0 = setup is one clause, or the setup is genuinely interesting on its own terms. Reward the diagnosis of reverse-engineered scaffolding, not length as such.
selected.rationale: R01 and R55 are the same 'super-calloused fragile mystic hexed by halitosis' construction with three back-filled paragraphs (diet, thinness, calluses) and are dense_pct .276 and .075 against card_pct .772 and .785. R40 builds an 'aqua-thermal treatment on ceramics' paragraph solely to reveal dishwashing, and R41 is a four-line verse existing only for 'it's snot' - both dense-low, card-high. Long visible craft is precisely what a rubric bank measures well and what the dense model discounts.

selected.name: Inventive taboo handling
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a sensitive or offensive premise is subordinated to an original joke mechanism; score 0 when shock value or the target supplies essentially all the humor.
selected.rationale: R16, R27, R37, R39, and R59 use religious, ethnic, tragic, or historical targets, making the distinction between mechanism and provocation salient.
member_names: Transgressive target delivered in minimum words

selected.name: Platform self-awareness
selected.instruction: Score 10 when commentary on posting, reading, reposting, or forum behavior is itself part of the joke’s mechanism; score 0 when platform language is generic decoration.
selected.rationale: R09, R35, R39, and R46 use the forum context as material rather than merely as setting.
member_names: Insider fluency in the forum's own conventions
Insider meta about the forum and its own habits

selected.name: Evergreen Subject Matter
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the joke relies on universal, timeless human conditions. Score 0 if it is inextricably tied to a specific, temporary news cycle, election, or fleeting pop culture moment.
selected.rationale: The dense model heavily penalizes R25 (Hillary/Trump) and R39 (Lewinsky/Bernie), indicating a strong preference for evergreen content over dated political references that a scorecard might over-credit.
member_names: Dependence on a dated news cycle or named topical figure

selected.name: Subversion of Common Idioms
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the punchline takes a common phrase or idiom and provides a literal, alternate, or punny reinterpretation. Score 0 if standard language is used with no double-meaning or subversion.
selected.rationale: The dense model scores R22 (subverting a serious vow into a Rickroll) and R29 (umbrella/brella/hesitation) highly. The scorecard seems to miss the clever phonetic or cultural subversion of these phrases.

selected.name: Distinctive speaker persona
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the speaker has a clear attitude or character whose voice materially contributes to the joke; score 0 when the statement could be delivered by anyone without change.
selected.rationale: R10, R17, R44, and R57 foreground recognizable speakers with specific attitudes, relationships, or self-presentations.

selected.name: The item performs the thing it describes
selected.instruction: Score whether the text enacts its own content rather than merely reporting it. 10 = the item's form is the joke -- it demonstrates, in the act of being read, exactly the phenomenon it names, and the enactment is the only place the humour lives. 5 = the item gestures at self-reference without actually doing anything. 0 = purely descriptive; the text makes a claim and the claim is not embodied in the text's own behaviour.
selected.rationale: The slice contains several enactment gags and the two models split on them: R30 (a sentence about what the speaker will never do, which turns into the Rickroll lyric and thereby does it) and R54 (a passage about nothing being new, quoted from the oldest available source) are dense-high, while R43 (a complaint about reposts, printed twice) and R28 ('read this aloud and you'll hear it') and R53 (one more shit post before the decade ends) are scorecard-high and dense-low. Enactment is invisible to criteria that score the proposition rather than the artefact, so the bank grades all five on their stated content.
member_names: Form enacts the joke AND carries a real second meaning
The item performs the thing it describes

selected.name: Clean lexical pivot
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a specific word or phrase legitimately supports two meanings and the final wording cleanly activates the second; score 0 when there is no pivot or the association is forced.
selected.rationale: R01, R36, and R46 use recognizable lexical pivots, whereas R14 and R44 show strained or underdeveloped word-based connections.
member_names: Surprise word occupies the final position

selected.name: Relatability of Frustration
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the joke taps into a widely shared everyday annoyance or social dynamic (addiction to scrolling, disappointment in content, petty logic) that readers feel personally. Score 0 if the premise is artificial or inaccessible.
selected.rationale: R12 (wanting to do something more when told not to), R28 (gaming free desserts), and R54 (following r/jokes despite disappointment) channel universal impulses the dense model rates highly. The scorecard may not weight 'this is me' resonance.

selected.name: Chestnut familiarity: reads as long-circulated stock material
selected.instruction: Score how fresh the item feels as a piece of writing, judged from internal signs of prior circulation: chain-email cadence, camp-rhyme meter, riddle-book phrasing, a punchline that is a decades-old set phrase, or an elaborate setup engineered backwards toward a famous pre-existing wordplay. 10 = the phrasing and construction feel newly written for this occasion; nothing about it reads as copied from a stock repertoire. 5 = a familiar joke type but freshly worded. 0 = unmistakably a warhorse -- a widely reproduced pun, rhyme, or chain-letter anecdote reproduced in its canonical form. Do not reward or punish quality; score only apparent circulation age.
selected.rationale: The slice contains the same museum-piece pun twice, in two different dressings -- R01 (Gandhi as 'super-calloused fragile mystic hexed by halitosis') and R16 (a monk, same punchline) -- and the scorecard rates both in its top quartile while the dense model rates both near its floor. R40 (the 'aqua-thermal treatment on ceramics' dishwashing chain-email) and R47 (the 'don't think it's funny 'cause it's snot' camp rhyme) show the same signature. A craft-property bank scores the well-machined construction and cannot see that the machine was built long ago and shown many times.
member_names: Chestnut familiarity: reads as long-circulated stock material
Reads as a canonical, already-in-circulation set text

selected.name: Form-dependent delivery
selected.instruction: Score 10 when repetition, typography, filenames, or read-aloud instructions materially create the joke; score 0 when the same joke works unchanged as plain prose.
selected.rationale: R04, R25, and R43 make presentation format part of the semantic or comic device.

selected.name: Phonetic double-use
selected.instruction: Score 10 when sound similarity creates two clear meanings that are quickly recoverable; score 0 when there is no phonetic mechanism or the resemblance is strained.
selected.rationale: R05, R34, and R54 rely on sound-based transformations that a broad checklist may treat as ordinary wordplay.

selected.name: Whole-setup re-parse versus bare homophone swap
selected.instruction: For items containing wordplay, score how much of the setup is retroactively re-read. 10 = the second meaning forces the reader to reinterpret the entire preceding sentence, which turns out to have been true in two ways at once. 5 = the pivot word carries two meanings but only the immediate phrase re-reads. 0 = the wordplay is a phonetic substitution -- one word that merely sounds like another -- with no second coherent reading of the setup. Items with no wordplay score 0.
selected.rationale: R41 (the umbrella inventor 'hesitated' -- the whole anecdote re-reads), R50 (a UDP joke you might not receive -- the protocol and the gag are the same object), R51 (no X and I know Y) sit dense-high. The scorecard-high side is thick with pure sound-swaps that re-read nothing: R03 ('put it on the record'), R58 ('Re:LAX'), R08 ('reception'), R36 ('a shift of wit'). A bank that scores 'contains a pun' or 'wordplay quality' counts both kinds equally and therefore over-credits the shallower half.
member_names: Whole-setup re-parse versus bare homophone swap

selected.name: Semantic snap precision
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the final wording delivers an immediate, exact reinterpretation with no filler; score 0 when there is no discernible payoff or it is vague.
selected.rationale: R01, R10, and R53 show compact jokes whose effect depends on an exact final word or phrase.

selected.name: Register-of-taboo content intensity
selected.instruction: 0-10: how much explicit sexual, scatological, slur-adjacent, or dark/shock subject matter does the item contain? Score extent of taboo content present in the text only; do not judge whether the taboo content is used tastefully, effectively, or is itself funny.
selected.rationale: R02 (explicit sexual content), R26 (contraception via 'being ugly'), R36 ('bucket full of shit') and R53 (scatological 'take a dump') all lean on shock/taboo material that can drive votes through provocation rather than construction quality, though taboo subject matter can also be genuinely well-crafted, hence mixed.

selected.name: Meta-forum and audience-management furniture
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text contains direct addresses to the forum (e.g., 'Reddit', 'this sub', 'r/jokes'), references to posting/upvoting mechanics (e.g., 'front page', 'upvotes'), or explicit repost disclaimers. Do not judge whether this makes the joke good or bad.
selected.rationale: Mentions of the forum or posting mechanics act as a textual fingerprint for an author ingrained in the community, which can drive engagement independently of the joke's intrinsic humor. Cites R02, R14.

selected.name: Canonical-chestnut retelling fingerprint (position in retelling chain)
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text presents as a re-rendering of a joke, pun, rhyme or lyric that already circulates widely, rather than as newly minted: a stock template filled in, wording that reads as the standard version of a known gag, an old schoolyard rhyme or a well-worn pun form, an explicit signal that the item has been seen before ('technically a repost', a line deliberately repeated verbatim), or a payoff that assumes the reader already knows the original. 0 = reads as freshly written for this posting; 10 = reads as a faithful retelling of an already-circulating item. Score the retelling signals in the text only. Do NOT judge whether retelling is lazy or whether the item is funny, and do not check whether it is actually a repost.
selected.rationale: MODE 3 channel: where an item sits in a joke's circulation history is invisible metadata, but it leaves textual traces a judge can score. The slice contains a literal collision — R04 and R09 are two independent renderings of the same 'super-calloused fragile mystic hexed by halitosis' pun — plus R10, which enacts a repost by printing its own sentence twice, R59, which declares itself a repost in the text, and stock chestnuts rendered in near-standard form at R46 ('I'm on a seafood diet'), R57 (the 'it's snot' rhyme) and R39 (verbatim Rickroll lyrics). Mixed because heavy circulation can itself be evidence that a joke works.

selected.name: Era-dating topical and platform-idiom references
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text is pinned to a specific period by its references: named politicians, celebrities, companies or products in a then-current situation, a named news event, a calendar moment ('the end of the decade'), platform slang or internet-meme idiom that belongs to a particular stretch of the web, or a joke form that was a fad at some moment. 0 = timeless content that could have been written in any year; 10 = the item cannot be read without placing it in a particular period. Score how strongly the text dates itself. Do NOT judge whether the reference is stale, fresh, or funny.
selected.rationale: MODE 3 channel: the posting date is unseen but leaves an unmistakable textual fingerprint, and it can only be a nuisance channel because the crowd verdict is defined within comparison pools rather than by epoch. Examples span several eras: R30 (Monica Lewinsky voting for Bernie against a Clinton), R51 (Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump), R08 (Elon Musk siting a new Tesla factory), R03 ('before the end of the decade'), R52 ('this one weird trick' clickbait idiom), R39 (Rickroll), R16 (Eid falling on 9/11).

selected.name: Orthographic-noise signature
selected.instruction: Using only the item text, score 0-10 for how much it contains unusual capitalization, spelling errors, punctuation runs, underscores, markdown artifacts, hashtags, handles, spacing anomalies, or other typographic noise; do not judge whether the feature is good or funny.
selected.rationale: Posting device, editing care, or platform formatting can leave highly learnable visual residue that is unrelated to joke quality. R02 contains hash marks and an unusual line break, while R26 has conspicuous capitalization and misspellings.

selected.name: Clean commitment to one recognised joke format
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the item commits cleanly to a single recognised delivery format and stops: pick the format it is attempting (one-liner, question-and-answer riddle, difference-between riddle, two-hander dialogue, numbered steps, narrative build) and score how completely the text conforms to that template with one set-up, one punch seam, and no trailing commentary, second punch, or explanatory tail after the punch. 0 = no identifiable format, or a format abandoned partway, or substantial text continuing past the punch; 10 = a textbook-clean instance of one template ending exactly at its punch. Score conformity to template shape only. You must NOT judge whether the punch lands, whether the format is over-used, or whether the joke is good.
selected.rationale: MODE 4 channel: practice at the format is upstream of both template-cleanliness and, plausibly, genuine quality, so it is tagged mixed. Template conformity is nonetheless a shape statistic rather than a verdict, and it splits the slice: R21, R40, R47 and R56 are textbook question-and-answer riddles, R42 is a clean scripted two-hander, and R46 is clean numbered steps, whereas R38 sprawls into a run-on with a post-punch tail ('Just makes sense really'), R27 stacks two punches after an aside, and R33 and R59 abandon their format before completing it.

selected.name: Unedited or non-US-native English surface traces
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of surface traces of little proofreading or of English written outside a US-native register: misspellings and letter transpositions, wrong or missing punctuation and capitalisation, duplicated or garbled words, non-US spellings ('aluminium'), formal or bookish connectives ('On further enquiry', 'All-in-all'), and phrasing that reads as translated or as second-language idiom. 0 = clean, idiomatic, evidently proofread US-native prose; 10 = pervasive traces. Score only the visible surface traces. Do NOT judge whether the errors are endearing, sloppy, or whether they hurt or help the joke, and do not judge the joke.
selected.rationale: Proofreading effort and language background are upstream of the text and leave a legible orthographic fingerprint, yet neither is what the crowd is voting on. Traces are frequent here: R24 ('2 areials', 'recpetion'), R09 ('Ghandi Mahatma Gandhi' — name emitted twice), R04 ('callouses'), R56 ('aluminium', 'On further enquiry', 'I was impressed......'), R34 (all-lowercase, no punctuation), R37 (stilted 'I always had troubles with people talking to me'), R23 ('the spend all their time').

selected.name: Multi-line narrative build-up length
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the item uses a multi-paragraph or multi-line structure with an extended narrative build-up before the punchline, rather than a one-liner or two-line Q&A. Do not judge the pacing quality.
selected.rationale: Longer, multi-line formats leave textual fingerprints of authorial effort or copy-pasting from external joke sites, which might influence reader perception differently than pithy one-liners. Cites R39, R41.

selected.name: Recognized classic retelling or known pun
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text relies on a widely known, highly circulated joke template or setup (e.g., the 'super calloused fragile mystic' pun) without subverting expectations. Judge only the obvious presence of an established classic setup, not the quality.
selected.rationale: Items that are recognizable classic formats might get upvotes from nostalgia or recognition rather than novel humor, acting as a spurious circulation channel. Cites R21, R48.
